sentence: Gestational diabetes is a form of diabetes that starts during pregnancy.
Diabetes UK describes it as affecting women who did not have diabetes before, and it typically clears up after the baby is born.
During pregnancy the placenta produces hormones that can interfere with the way insulin works.
Insulin is the hormone that helps the body handle sugar in the blood.
When it works less well, the body struggles to use insulin well and blood sugar can rise.
Some people are more likely to develop it than others, and the NHS lists the factors that raise the chance.

These include a higher BMI, having had gestational diabetes before, a previous large baby, a parent or sibling with diabetes, and a South Asian, Black, African-Caribbean or Middle Eastern family background.
The NHS adds that this applies even to people who were born in the UK.
These are factors that change the chance, not signs that anyone did something wrong.
note: Interpretive framing of the NHS risk list; not stated verbatim.

sentence: NICE notes that the risks can be reduced but not removed completely.
Most people with gestational diabetes have no symptoms.
It is usually found when blood sugar is tested during screening in pregnancy.

sentence: When blood sugar runs high, people may notice extra thirst, passing urine more often, especially at night, a dry mouth, tiredness or blurred vision.

sentence: Genital itching or thrush can also occur.
Having one of these symptoms does not necessarily mean someone has gestational diabetes.
note: NHS inform wording in search text.

Diabetes UK says it is usually diagnosed from a blood test taken during pregnancy.
Because symptoms are often absent, screening is how most cases are found.

sentence: Screening begins at the booking appointment, when the midwife or doctor asks questions to work out whether someone has an increased risk.
Women with a higher risk are offered a blood test called an oral glucose tolerance test.
The NHS and Diabetes UK describe this test as taking place between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy.
Women who have had gestational diabetes before are offered a test earlier, soon after the booking appointment, and a second one later if the first is normal.

NICE guidance lists obesity, a previous history of gestational diabetes, a close relative with diabetes, a previous large baby and an ethnicity with a high rate of diabetes among the risk factors used.
note: Search text on NICE NG3 recommendations (blended with NHS trust text).

sentence: Guidance can differ a little between regions, so local maternity teams explain their own arrangements.
Treatment starts with changes to diet and physical activity.
The NHS describes swapping sugary snacks and drinks for alternatives, and notes that some fruit juices, smoothies and drinks labelled no added sugar can still be high in sugar.
Regular physical activity is part of the advice as well.
note: NHS and Diabetes UK say diet and exercise.

sentence: Medicine may be offered if blood sugar is still not stable 1 to 2 weeks after those changes, or if it is very high at diagnosis.
The options are tablets, usually metformin, or insulin injections.
Diabetes UK says metformin helps reduce the glucose the liver produces and makes insulin work better.
Insulin is given by injection and may be recommended if metformin cannot be taken, causes side effects or does not lower blood sugar enough.
The NHS says birth should take place at a hospital where specially trained staff can care for the baby.
During labour, blood sugar is monitored and kept under control, and insulin may be given through a drip.

sentence: Medicines for gestational diabetes are usually stopped straight after the birth.

sentence: Blood sugar is tested again to check that it has returned to normal.
The NHS recommends a blood test to check for diabetes 6 to 13 weeks after the birth.
This matters because a small number of women continue to have raised blood sugar after pregnancy.

If the result is normal, the NHS advises a yearly test, because gestational diabetes increases the chance of type 2 diabetes, a lifelong form of diabetes.
NICE also advises continuing lifestyle advice and a yearly HbA1c test, and says future pregnancies should include diabetes testing.
